title: The survival of the luxury Swiss watchmaking business

paragraphs.text: These days, no one requires a Swiss watch to tell the time – or a watch from any country. The time displayed on our mobile phones and other digital devices will always be more accurate than the time displayed on even the most skilfully engineered mechanical watch. Yet the Swiss watch industry has a visual presence in our lives like few others. The storefronts of the world’s big-money boulevards have rows of Swiss watches with their manufacturers prominently displayed; magazines appear to be kept in business largely by glossy watch adverts; airport duty-free shops tempt passers-by with expensive models. The export value of the Swiss watch trade is up 62.9% compared with six years ago, with some watches going for over £2 million each.

In the last century, we experienced the invention of the atomic clock, the internet, and pixelated clocks constantly flashing on our computers and phones. And yet none of these developments has threatened the dominance of the Swiss watchmaking industry. This raises a string of questions. Why was it Switzerland in the first place? How did this unassuming, landlocked country come to dominate the industry? And how did it master the art of charging tens of thousands of pounds for an object that often kept time less accurately than an object costing £10?

In fact, the first mechanical watches were not Swiss. The earliest - first round and then oval-shaped, and worn as large necklaces – appeared around 1510 in Germany, the Netherlands, France and Italy. A small trade developed in Switzerland a few decades later, thanks largely to artisans employed as goldsmiths. The experience of these craftsmen with intricate engraving tools enabled them to turn their attention to miniature mechanics. But companies based in France and Germany were also producing prized specimens at this time.

However, the Swiss just kept on going, occasionally buying up the most prominent firms elsewhere in Europe, and forming trade bodies and certification targets that increased the industry’s reputation for quality and honesty. In the 19th century, the Swiss became masters of the new mechanisms that enabled traditional watches to evolve into wristwatches. They made full use of new innovations, replacing the old method of winding a watch by inserting a key with the modern mechanism still used to manually wind watches today. In the early 20th century, they combined the new American-originated system of conveyor-belt mechanisation with the finest methods of local handcrafting. Soon they had gained a worldwide reputation for precision and beauty.

All went well until the 1970s, when the mechanical watch trade faced a major threat with the development by an American company, Timex, of a watch that ran on quartz. It contained a tiny piece of quartz crystal that resonated at a fixed frequency when powered by a battery. This steady signal was then transmitted to an electronic circuit which regulated the gears that turned the watch hands. The old mechanism which involved winding your watch every night was dismissed at a stroke.

The quartz movement had been around since the 1920s, but its miniaturisation had only been achieved in Japan in the late 1960s. Its price had previously taken it beyond the general consumer, but now, through mass production in America, the electronic watch represented a change of philosophy. Split-second timing, once the exclusive domain of physicists and technicians, was now available to all, and there was no better symbol of the major shift from the mechanical to the electronic world.

The Swiss reacted to the digital disruption with a combination of denial and mild panic. Between 1970 and 1983, the Swiss share of the watch market fell from 50% to 15%, and the industry shed more than half its workforce. But the Swiss fought back with a new philosophy of their own, something colourful, cheap and powered by quartz and battery: the Swatch, which made watches desirable again for a new generation. The Swatch Group is now the world’s largest watchmaking company.

But the luxury end of the market continues to thrive. Making anything really small by hand tends to be extremely expensive. In the luxury watch industry, the precision of the tiny parts is one reason for the great cost (even the tiniest screw costs eight Swiss francs, precisely because it is such a tiny screw). But the major contributory factor is human and centuries-old: the wisdom handed down through the generations that is required to make something beautiful and functional from an otherwise inanimate assemblage of metal and stones.

Once you can afford to spend even entry-level prices on a luxury watch, your watch has begun to represent status and one-upmanship. Something glittery on your wrist says something about your earning power and your taste, much as an expensive car can do; it is not always an attractive trait, It’s a delusion, of course, but the more complicated and expensive the watch, the more the wearer may assume control of the universe, the still centre of a spinning wheel.

And perhaps there is something else ticking away before us – a feeling that the acceleration of our daily lives may soon prove overwhelming. When watchmaking began, we had no concept of packed calendars and unbreakable deadlines, much less of ‘quality time’ or ‘me time’ These days, having brought this ungovernable storm of rush upon ourselves, we may be grateful for anything – not least a beautiful timepiece – that reinstates at least an illusion of control.
